newsitem.title: UK: Power blackout paralyses London Underground system.
newsitem.headline: Power blackout paralyses London Underground system.

text.p: London's underground train service was paralysed by a power failure for 2-1/2 hours on Wednesday night, leaving thousands of passengers stranded in tunnels and stations.
A spokesman for London Underground, operators of the system, said the power cut had affected most of the system. Passengers and station officials said the whole system had ground to a halt.
Domestic and other commercial electricity supplies in the city were not affected.

Stations were closed to travellers who were told to find other means of transport after the power cut at 9:45 p.m. (same GMT). Passengers already waiting in stations were led out but those on trains had to wait for the power to be reconnected.

Once power was restored at 00:13 a.m. on Thursday, trains pulled into the next station where passengers disembarked. Most of them then had to find their way home by other means in a city where most of the public transport shuts down overnight, leaving only a skeleton night bus service.
There were no reports of any injuries.

Central London was packed with bewildered tourists and residents leaving restaurants, cinemas and theatres who were faced with a long wait to travel home on a freezing night. Long queues built up for buses and taxis.
"As far as we can see, we will be able to operate normally tomorrow," a London Underground spokesman said.

Television stations said the problem was caused by a breakdown at a power station supplying the "Tube" system. The underground network comprises 11 lines that criss-cross Europe's biggest city and transport 2.7 million people a day.
In April a power failure -- which officials then called the worst ever -- hit the Underground, trapping passengers in trains and causing chaos for Easter tourists and sports fans.
Ambulance services said 31 people were treated in hospital for smoke inhalation when a train failed at busy Earl's Court station in west London during the April power cut.
Passenger groups have warned the government that lack of investment in the Underground system could have serious long-term effects. The Underground has 248 stations and employs around 16,000 staff.
